asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice gets a planet and one of the small cards. Your Sun falls in the last ten degrees of Cancer, somewhere from 20 to 29. In the Golden Dawn order this slice goes to the Moon, and the Moon rules Cancer, so here it's at home, working in its own house with nothing to push against. That's less common than you'd think. The first slice of Cancer belongs to Venus and the Two of Cups, two people swapping cups, which is Cancer at its most openly affectionate. The middle slice is Mercury's, the Three of Cups, friends with their cups raised, the chatty and sociable side of the sign. Yours is the quietest of the three. It's Cancer ripening, cardinal water that has done most of its moving and is already leaning towards Leo next door. The Chariot is your Sun card, the broad picture of Cancer, and the Four of Cups is the finer grain inside it.

You notice everything and say about a third of it. At a friend's birthday drinks you can tell within ten minutes who's had a bad week, and you'll end up in the corner with them while the rest of the table carries on. Afterwards you need a whole Sunday with nothing in it, the phone face down, a pot of something on the stove. A message from your mum can sit unanswered for two days, and it isn't that you don't care. You're waiting until you've got the room in you to answer it properly. When someone asks what you'd like for dinner you honestly might not know, because you've been tuned to what everyone else wanted all day. People who've known you a while learn to leave the quiet alone, and to trust that you'll come back round in your own time.

The less obvious gift is that you're hard to sell things to. When a job offer turns up with a bigger salary and everyone around you says take it, you'll sit with it for a week and quite often turn it down, and a year later it's usually clear you read it right. Look at the figure on your card, arms folded, three cups lined up and a fourth being held out from a cloud. Most people see boredom there. I tend to see someone who knows what they've already got and isn't about to grab at the next thing because it's shiny. You're also the one who remembers. A friend mentioned her father's operation once, in passing, eight months ago, and you're the person who asks how he's going, and asks about him by name.

The harder thing is what you decide while you're in your shell. When your mood drops, and with the Moon this strong it does drop, the job, the flat and sometimes the partner all start to look like the problem. You can draft a resignation letter on a grey Thursday that you'd never have written on a good Monday. Then there are the invitations. You say no to the barbecue, then the weekend away, then a birthday, each for a decent reason, and after the third time people stop asking. Then you feel left out, and a bit hurt, though nobody did anything wrong. Some of that is Cancer wanting to be chased a little. It's worth knowing that about yourself, because most friends won't think to do the chasing.

When something goes badly, a breakup, a redundancy, a death in the family, your first move is to go home and close the door. You cancel things, you cook the same comfort meal three nights running, and you tell people you're fine in a voice that makes it clear you'd like them to leave it there. A week later you're often still in, but now you're going over it, replaying old conversations, sometimes ones from years back, trying to find where it went wrong. The people around you can feel shut out, especially a partner who wanted to help and wasn't allowed. What helps is small and physical. Someone turning up with food and no need to talk, a walk by water, a bath, sleep at proper hours. Then, once you've had a few days, one honest phone call to the person you've been avoiding.

In love you're often the one looking after everyone, and you're honestly not great at being looked after back. A partner makes you dinner or books a weekend away and you can find yourself slightly awkward about it, wondering what they'll want in return. That's the fourth cup on your card, if we're being straight about it, the care that's being held out while you're busy with the three you've already lined up. You also tend to go quiet when you're hurt and then wait to see if they notice. Sometimes they do. Plenty of decent partners don't, because they simply can't read the signal, and you end up feeling unloved by someone who loves you a great deal. It helps to say it in words, even clumsily. "I'm upset about Saturday and I need you to ask me about it" is enough.

Work tends to go well for you when it means looking after something over a long stretch. Nursing, teaching, hospitality, a family business, an archive, anything with a long memory. You'd sooner keep one client for ten years than chase a new one every week, and you're very good at picking up what a customer or a team needs before they've said it. The difficulty is that a job can go flat on you without warning. The same role you loved for four years can feel like nothing at all one Monday, and you won't always know why. Before you walk out, check whether it's the job or your own tide going out. Give it a month. If it's still flat, look at what's already being offered, the side project, the transfer, the course your manager mentioned, because with this decan the next thing is usually on the table somewhere.

At twenty this slice of Cancer is often quite hard on itself. You feel a lot and assume everyone else is coping better, and there can be a stretch of staying in your room, turning down things you later wish you'd gone to. By the mid-thirties most people with this decan have learnt their own rhythm. They know the low weeks come and go, they stop making big decisions inside them, and they've usually built a home that works as a proper place to recover. The Leo next door starts to show a bit too, some warmth in company, a bit less hiding. The fifties tend to bring an ease with it all. A lot of late Cancers I've seen end up as the family's memory, the one who keeps the photos and the recipes and knows who fell out with whom at the 1987 Christmas.

Keep a short list on your phone called 'offered'. Each time someone holds something out to you, an invitation, a compliment, help with the move, a lead on a job, write it down in a few words, whether you took it or not. Once a month, on the full moon if you like that sort of thing, read back through it. Pick one thing you let pass and go back to the person about it. Ask if it still stands, or just thank them properly.
